title: Context Matters
text:
Key Takeaways






Context is all the information you give an LLM to understand your request (role, purpose, audience, requirements)
Be specific, not vague — clear context gets relevant responses; vague prompts get generic ones
Refine iteratively — start basic, review the output, add details, repeat until satisfied
Never share sensitive personal information with AI tools, even if the task seems straightforward










🦆 Warm-up activity with duck.ai



Open duck.ai and send this minimal prompt:

Write me a report about managing Type 2 diabetes

Then immediately send a follow-up prompt that adds context:

I am a community nurse preparing a 1-page briefing for patients about managing Type 2 diabetes at home. Please write a clear, accessible summary suitable for someone with no medical background.

The first prompt will likely produce a very generic response—possibly asking you to clarify, or generating a template so broad it is almost useless. The second prompt, with clear context, should produce something targeted and practical.


Large Language Models work by navigating through vast embedding spaces—multidimensional representations of knowledge and concepts. Vague or poorly defined context can lead the model to explore irrelevant areas of this space, producing generic or off-target responses. Well-crafted context act as precise navigation instructions, guiding the model to the most relevant knowledge areas and ensuring outputs that match your specific needs and context.



Multidimensional embedding space example.



Why Context Matters for LLMs
Context is everything you provide to an LLM to help it understand your request and generate appropriate responses within your session. Without proper context, LLMs often produce generic, inaccurate, or inappropriate outputs.
Because LLMs have no memory between separate sessions, they have no knowledge of who you are, your organisation’s policies, or the purpose of your request unless you tell them.
Example of poor context:

Write me a report about productivity

Example of better context:

I am a team lead in a mid-sized technology company. I need to write a 2-page summary about remote work productivity for our department heads, focusing on evidence-based strategies and including practical implementation steps for hybrid teams.







A note on privacy



While LLMs have no memory between separate chat sessions, the data you share within each session may be stored or used by the service provider. Always check the tool’s privacy policy before sharing any personal, confidential, or sensitive information.
When in doubt, anonymise or use placeholder data:
🚫 Do not share: personal records, health data, confidential business information, legal advice, passwords, or unpublished research
✅ Do share: general descriptions of your role, anonymised examples, publicly available context




Types of Context
Explicit Context — Information you directly provide, for example:

Your role and area of work
The purpose of the task
The intended audience

Implicit Context — Assumptions the LLM makes based on your prompt, for example:

Cultural background
Expected level of technical detail
Formality of language

The general principle we want to follow is making implicit context explicit. The more specific and detailed your context, the better the LLM can tailor its response to your needs.


Working Within Context Limits
LLMs have context windows—limits on how much text they can process at once. Some practical strategies:

Summarise lengthy background information and prioritise what is most essential
Break complex tasks into smaller, sequential steps
Use previous outputs as context for follow-up requests (within the same session)



Iterative Context Building
You will rarely get the ideal result on the first attempt. A productive strategy is to start simple and refine:

Initial request: Provide core context
Review output: Identify what is missing or off-target
Refine context: Add specific details or correct misunderstandings
Iterate: Repeat until the output meets your needs




Exercise 2: Context Writing
Scenario: You are volunteering at a community food bank. You need to create a guide about healthy eating for a low-income community group in your area.
Task: Start with the minimal prompt below, observe the output, then craft an improved version with full context and compare the results in duck.ai.
Initial prompt:

Write a guide about healthy eating







Solution example





Contextualised prompt

Context: I am a volunteer coordinator for a community food bank serving low-income families in an urban neighbourhood. Many members are under financial pressure and may have limited access to fresh produce.
Purpose: Create a practical, encouraging guide to eating healthily on a tight budget—without making people feel judged about their circumstances.
Audience: Adults of mixed literacy levels; some may have limited English. Keep language simple and avoid jargon.
Scope: Cover practical tips for affordable nutrition: meal planning, batch cooking, making use of frozen and tinned vegetables, and interpreting food labels. Exclude expensive “superfoods” or diet trends.
Format: One page with clear headings, short bullet points, and a friendly tone.

title: Ethics, Privacy & Fairness
text:
Key Takeaways






Transparency, human oversight, privacy, and fairness are the UNESCO principles most directly relevant to everyday AI use
You remain responsible for every output you act on or share, regardless of whether AI generated it
Never submit other people’s personal data to a commercial AI tool without checking the tool’s privacy policy and your right to share it
AI systems inherit societal biases — actively check outputs for bias rather than assuming they are neutral
Intellectual property questions around AI-generated content are unresolved — treat AI output as a draft requiring genuine human authorship










🦆 Warm-up activity with duck.ai



Open duck.ai and send this prompt:

Write me a brief summary of 5 influential political leaders in the 20th century

Review the output carefully. Are there any patterns in who is included or excluded? What assumptions or perspectives are embedded in the response? This exercise illustrates how AI outputs can reflect and amplify societal biases, making critical evaluation essential.
Now try:

Write me a brief summary of 5 influential political leaders in the 20th century from diverse regions, genders, and political perspectives.




Transparency
The UNESCO Recommendation places transparency at the heart of responsible AI use. Being transparent means acknowledging when AI has contributed to your work — whether you are drafting a document, writing a social media post, or preparing a report. Transparency is not about apologising for using AI; it is about honesty with your audience.


Human Oversight
UNESCO is explicit that humans must remain in control of decisions that affect people’s lives. AI must not be the final decision-maker in employment, healthcare, legal proceedings, education, or any other high-stakes context. This principle also operates at the individual level: you are responsible for any output you act on or share, even when AI generated it.


Privacy and Data Protection
When you use AI tools for work-related tasks, whether through web interfaces, APIs, or integrated applications, your data typically:

Travels over the internet to AI company servers
Gets processed by AI systems you don’t control

May be stored temporarily or permanently by the AI provider
Could potentially be used for training future AI models
Might be subject to different legal jurisdictions

Understanding this data flow is crucial for making informed decisions about what information you share with AI systems, especially when handling sensitive data or proprietary content. Always evaluate these risks and follow the law and any guidance from your organisation regarding AI use and data sharing.






What not to submit to a commercial AI tool



🚫 Other people’s personal information — names, addresses, health data, financial details
🚫 Information shared with you in confidence — medical, legal, or personal disclosures
🚫 Unpublished work or commercially sensitive material
🚫 Passwords, API keys, or security credentials
🚫 Any content you would not be comfortable seeing in a data breach


When choosing an AI tool for tasks involving sensitive information, look for a clear and readable privacy policy, the ability to opt out of training data collection, and compliance with data protection law in your country (such as GDPR in the UK and EU). For learning and general use, privacy-respecting tools such as duck.ai provide a good default — DuckDuckGo does not save conversations or use inputs for model training.


Fairness and Non-Discrimination
AI systems are trained on data that reflects the inequalities and prejudices present in society. They can reproduce and amplify those biases in ways that are subtle and difficult to detect — particularly because the outputs look fluent and authoritative.
Common patterns to watch for include gender bias (associating professions or leadership with particular genders), racial and ethnic bias (stereotypical associations or underrepresentation of certain groups), socioeconomic bias (assuming access to resources or education), and geographic bias (centring Western, English-speaking perspectives as the default).






Bias detection questions



When reviewing any AI output, ask:

Representation: Who is included in the examples, and who is absent?
Language: Are descriptions fair and respectful to all groups?
Assumptions: What unstated assumptions are embedded in the response?
Perspectives: Whose viewpoint is centred, and whose is absent?
Stereotypes: Are any harmful generalisations present?



Producing more equitable outputs requires deliberate prompting — explicitly requesting diverse examples, asking for multiple perspectives, and challenging responses that default to a narrow worldview. Even then, the model’s knowledge of underrepresented groups is often shallower and less reliable, making independent verification more important, not less.


Intellectual Property
AI-generated content raises questions about ownership and copyright. Under UK law, works created by AI without human authorship may not attract copyright protection. If you use AI to assist with creating materials, you remain responsible for:

Rights to any source material used
Avoiding infringement of third-party IP
Acknowledging AI use where required by academic integrity policies

The most reliable approach is to treat AI outputs as drafts requiring genuine human authorship: revise substantively, add your own analysis and judgement, and attribute AI assistance where your context requires it.


The Human Dimensions of AI
Beyond the formal principles, responsible use also involves asking what is lost — not just what is gained — when AI takes over a task.
LLM training relies on human labellers who evaluate outputs and identify harmful content, work known as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). This labour is frequently outsourced to workers in lower-income countries, often under precarious conditions. The benefits of AI accrue largely to wealthy technology companies and their users; the costs are disproportionately borne by others.
There is also a question about authenticity in human communication. Using AI to generate a response to a heartfelt message from a colleague or friend may signal — consciously or not — that their communication did not warrant genuine attention. And in learning and professional contexts, the process of writing and thinking has value that is separate from the quality of the finished product. Delegating that process to AI can produce an acceptable document while eroding the expertise that comes from doing the work yourself.

These are not reasons to avoid AI. They are reasons to choose deliberately.

title: Summary
text:
What You Have Covered
Congratulations on completing Harnessing AI. Here is a summary of the key ideas:
What are LLMs? LLMs predict the most likely next word based on patterns in vast training data. They work by pattern matching, not true understanding. They can hallucinate, carry bias, and make mistakes — and these limitations are not “bugs” but fundamental properties of how they work.
Context Matters. Vague prompts produce generic outputs. Providing clear context — who you are, what you need, for whom, in what format — consistently produces more useful results. Never share personal, confidential, or sensitive information with AI tools.
Prompting Frameworks. Structured prompting reduces wasted effort and improves output quality.
Conversational Learning. LLMs work best as thinking partners in multi-turn conversations. You can steer, correct, and challenge the model across multiple exchanges.
Responsible Use of AI. The UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI (2021) provides a universal framework grounded in human rights, fairness, transparency, human oversight, privacy, and environmental sustainability. These principles apply to everyone who uses AI — not just developers and policymakers.
Ethics & Environmental Impact. AI has a real environmental footprint. It inherits and can amplify societal biases. It raises questions about authentic human communication, labour practices, and intellectual property. Use AI where it adds genuine value; choosing not to use it is always a legitimate option.






Your responsible AI checklist



Before using an AI tool for any significant task:

✅ Verify: Do not act on specific facts, citations, or statistics without independent verification
✅ Protect privacy: Do not submit personal data about yourself or others without checking the tool’s privacy policy
✅ Maintain oversight: You are responsible for every output you share or act on — review carefully
✅ Be transparent: Attribute AI assistance where your context requires it
✅ Consider the human dimension: Would the people affected feel respected by this use of AI?
✅ Think proportionately: Is the task genuinely worth the energy, privacy, and relational costs involved?




Good luck, and use AI thoughtfully.

title: Prompting Frameworks
text:
Key Takeaways






High-quality prompts eliminate ambiguity — clear context upfront gets better responses
Structured frameworks like CLEAR help ensure your prompt is complete
There is no single “correct” framework — use what works best for you and your context
Never share personal, confidential, or sensitive information in any prompt




We can use some frameworks to standardize our queries and make sure they are complete and don’t forget any relevant details. There’s no right or wrong approach — different frameworks may work better for different AI tools and yourself, so use the one that works better for you.

The CLEAR Framework
High-quality prompts eliminate ambiguity. By providing comprehensive context upfront, you are more likely to receive output that matches your requirements without multiple rounds of correction.
The CLEAR framework offers a systematic approach to prompt construction:
C — Context: Establish the situation and background

Explain who you are and what you are working on
Provide relevant background about your project or domain
Include any important constraints or considerations

L — Length: Define output requirements

Specify how much content you want (word count, number of items, etc.)
Indicate format preferences (paragraphs, bullet points, structured sections)
Include any structural requirements

E — Examples: Illustrate desired outcomes

Show examples of the style or format you are looking for
Provide sample inputs or scenarios when relevant
Include both positive examples (what you want) and negative examples (what to avoid)

A — Action: State the specific task

Clearly articulate what you want the AI to do
Use specific action verbs (create, analyse, summarise, compare, explain)
Be direct and avoid ambiguous language
Focus on one primary task per prompt

R — Role: Define the AI’s perspective

Specify what expertise or viewpoint the AI should adopt
Indicate the audience the AI should write for
Guide the AI’s tone and decision-making approach


Example applying CLEAR framework
Scenario: You manage social media for a local charity supporting elderly people living alone and want to write a recruitment post for volunteers.

Context: I manage communications for a small charity that runs a befriending service for elderly people living alone. We want to recruit new telephone volunteers—people who call a lonely older person once a week for a friendly chat.
Length: Write a 200-word recruitment post with a short headline.
Examples: Use a warm, human tone—similar to this: “Last year, Sarah spent 20 minutes a week making calls that meant everything to someone who had no one else.” Avoid corporate language or guilt-tripping.
Action: Write a volunteer recruitment post for our charity’s Facebook page.
Role: Act as a charity communications officer who understands how to inspire volunteers through storytelling and empathy, not pressure.






Exercise 3: Building a Prompt with CLEAR
Scenario: You are planning a community workshop on digital skills for older adults.
Task: Use the CLEAR framework to write a prompt in duck.ai that asks for a 2-hour workshop agenda. Then reflect on the output:

Did the model follow your format requirements?
Was the level of detail appropriate for the audience you specified?
What would you change in your prompt to improve the output?







Solution example






Context: I am a librarian organising a free 2-hour digital skills workshop for adults aged 65 and over. Many participants will have little or no experience using smartphones or tablets. The workshop will be held at the local library with a maximum of 12 participants and one facilitator.
Length: Create a detailed 2-hour workshop agenda with 15–20 minute segments.
Examples: Include hands-on practice time after each concept is introduced, similar to this structure: introduce → demonstrate → participants try → debrief. No slide-heavy lectures.
Action: Design an agenda that progresses from very basic (turning a device on, navigating home screen) to practical tasks (sending a message, using video calls).
Role: Act as an experienced adult digital inclusion facilitator who understands common anxieties older adults have about technology.
Additional constraints: - Avoid technical jargon; explain everything in plain English - Include a comfort break - End with a Q&A and a list of local support resources participants can take home

title: Introduction
text:
Artificial Intelligence refers to computer systems that can perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence, such as understanding language, recognising patterns, and making decisions. While AI research has a long history, today’s widespread interest is driven largely by generative AI—systems that create new content such as text, images, and code based on patterns learned from vast amounts of data. You have probably heard of and used chatbot tools like ChatGPT, Copilot, or Claude. Here we will learn how to use Large Language Models (LLMs) effectively and responsibly.






Guiding Principles



This course is grounded in internationally recognised principles for responsible AI use, drawing on the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (2021)—the first global standard on AI ethics, adopted by 193 member states. Our approach emphasises:

Human dignity and rights: AI should serve people, not the other way around
Transparency: Being open about when and how AI is used
Critical thinking: Using AI to support, not replace, intellectual rigour
Fairness and inclusion: Being mindful of bias and ensuring equitable outcomes
Environmental responsibility: Recognising the ecological cost of AI use




Learning Objectives
By the end of this course, you will be able to:

Understand what LLMs are and their key capabilities and limitations
Apply responsible practices when using AI tools in your work or daily life
Craft effective prompts that enhance rather than replace critical thinking
Navigate ethical considerations including bias, privacy, and environmental impact
Understand the UNESCO framework for ethical AI use and how it applies to everyday decisions



About this course
These course materials have been designed and developed by Pau Erola, PhD (Jean Golding Institute, University of Bristol).
Thanks to Huw Day for his feedback and recommendations on ethics and environmental impact. Thanks to Leo Gorman, Will Chapman, Rita Rasteiro, Richard Lane, James Thomas and Patricia Holley for their valuable comments and corrections.
This course uses duck.ai as the hands-on AI tool for exercises—a privacy-respecting interface to LLMs provided by DuckDuckGo, which does not retain your conversations or use them for model training.
We used the enhancement of AI in alignment with our institutional guidance:

Microsoft Copilot (GPT-4 & GPT-5)– Generation of synthetic datasets, documents and examples
Claude (Sonnet 4) – Writing assistance, examples generation
ChatGPT (GPT-5) – Generation of figures

For queries related to this course please contact jgi-training@bristol.ac.uk.

title: What are LLMs?
text:
Key Takeaways






LLMs are mathematical models of language that map similar words to nearby positions in a conceptual space

They predict which words are most likely to follow a given input (prompt), based on patterns learned from vast amounts of text
They work by pattern matching, not true understanding—they are not infallible sources of truth

Always verify important information from authoritative sources
Be aware of bias in AI outputs and actively check for it
Use critical thinking: if something sounds too precise or too extreme, investigate further










🦆 Warm-up activity with duck.ai



Before reading further, open duck.ai and try the following prompt:

Complete this sentence in five different ways: “The bank was…”

Notice how the model generates different continuations based on the ambiguity of the word “bank”. This illustrates how LLMs rely on context and patterns to produce outputs, and why they can sometimes produce unexpected or incorrect results.



Natural Language Processing
Natural Language Processing (NLP) is a branch of Artificial Intelligence that serves as the foundational technology that enables Large Language Models to understand and generate human language. Natural language is inherently ambiguous and contextual.
Consider the sentence

“I saw the man with the telescope”.

This could mean:

you used a telescope to see the man,
or you saw a man carrying a telescope.

At its core, NLP transforms words, phrases, and sentences into numerical representations called embeddings — high-dimensional vectors that capture semantic meaning and relationships between linguistic elements. These embedding spaces are constructed so that words or phrases with similar meanings are positioned closer together in the vector space, while semantically different concepts are farther apart. For example, “king” and “man” would be nearby vectors, as would “queen” and “woman” but “man” and “woman” would be distant. This mathematical representation of language allows to perform some complex reasoning about text by manipulating these vectors through neural network operations.



A simple 2D embedding space of the words: blue, king, man, pink, princess, queen, woman.




The Large Language Model Revolution
Large Language Models represented a paradigm shift in learning language patterns from the Internet, books, and other vast text sources. Built on transformer architecture, LLMs focus on relevant parts of the input when processing words (tokens) or phrases, enabling understanding of long-range dependencies that earlier models missed. While you don’t need to understand the mathematics, the key insight is that LLMs work by finding patterns and relationships between concepts.
Let’s assume that we want to embed the words of this sentence:

The Jean Golding Institute is a central hub for data science and data-intensive research at the University of Bristol. We connect a multidisciplinary community of experts across the University and beyond.

Our chatbot will break the sentence in tokens of one or less words and assign each a numeric identifier, as depicted below. A rule of thumb is that one token generally corresponds to 4 characters of text for common English.




Text is broken into words or token. “A helpful rule of thumb is that one token generally corresponds to ~4 characters of text for common English text”. Source: https://platform.openai.com/tokenizer


Each of these tokens will have a mapping in the embedding space of our LLM model.



Multidimensional embedding space example.


What makes LLMs “large” is their training scale, the exposure to hundreds of billions of words from diverse sources allows them to internalize grammar, vocabulary, world knowledge, and reasoning patterns. The training process is elegantly simple: models learn by predicting the next word in sequences, adjusting internal parameters based on prediction errors. This forces development of sophisticated internal representations of language and knowledge.
LLMs fundamentally change how we approach NLP tasks. Instead of building specialized systems for each application, a single LLM can handle multiple tasks through different prompting strategies. The same model that excels at translation can also summarize documents, answer questions, or generate creative content without additional training.
The workplace implications are profound. Tasks requiring specialized software and technical expertise become accessible through natural language interaction. Document analysis, content generation, customer service automation, and data extraction are now available to non-technical users through conversational interfaces.


What can LLMs do?
LLMs can help with:

Writing assistance: Drafting emails, reports, and documents
Summarisation: Condensing long texts into key points
Translation: Converting between languages
Question answering: Providing information on a wide range of topics
Code generation: Writing and explaining programming code
Creative tasks: Brainstorming ideas and creative writing







Good Practice: AI as a thinking partner



AI should enhance your capabilities, not replace your thinking.


However, LLMs have important limitations:






LLM Limitations




Hallucinations: LLMs can generate plausible-sounding but entirely incorrect information.
Bias: LLMs reflect and can amplify biases present in their training data.
Mistakes: LLMs can make subtle errors that are difficult to detect without domain expertise.
No real-time knowledge: Most LLMs have a training cut-off and do not know about recent events unless they have web access.
No memory between sessions: Each new conversation starts from scratch unless memory features are explicitly enabled.



Why these limitations matter:

Personal and professional responsibility: Errors in your work—whether a report, an email, or a decision—can have serious consequences.
Integrity: Using unverified AI-generated content without disclosure undermines trust.
Ethical obligations: Propagating biased content can harm individuals and communities.







Why hallucinations are dangerous



The problem is not that LLMs make mistakes — so do humans. The problem is that hallucinations often sound exactly like correct answers. The model’s tone and formatting do not change when it is making something up. It may even cite a plausible-sounding paper that does not exist.
The Fake Citation
Open duck.ai and enter:

Give me three academic references (author, year, journal, title) about the effects of urban green spaces on mental health

Read the references carefully, then verify them.
The Invented Fact
Open duck.ai and enter:

Should we be eating less meat by 2030 to lower cancer risk?

Read the response carefully, then verify it.





Exercise 1: Identifying LLM Limitations
Scenario: You are preparing a briefing document about climate change impacts in your city.
Use duck.ai and enter the following prompt:

Write 2 sentences about how climate change is impacting [your city or region]

Then review the output and ask yourself:

Can you verify any specific statistics or dates?
Does the language sound overly confident about things that are uncertain?

Now compare your output with the three synthetic examples below and evaluate each one:

Write 2 sentences about how climate change is impacting Bristol


Output A: “Bristol experienced its wettest year on record in 2023, with rainfall 40% above average. The Severn Estuary’s sea level has risen 15cm since 2000, directly threatening the city centre.”

Output B: “Climate change will cause Bristol’s temperature to increase by exactly 3.2°C by 2050, making it uninhabitable for most residents. The city council has already approved plans to relocate the entire population to higher ground.”

Output C: “Bristol faces increased flooding risks due to climate change. The city has implemented various adaptation measures, though specific impacts vary by neighborhood and depend on global emission scenarios.”






Solution example





Output A — Contains specific statistics that need verification
⚠️ “Wettest year on record” and “40% above average” are precise claims requiring fact-checking against official sources
⚠️ “15cm since 2000” should be verified against peer-reviewed or government data
⚠️ Causal claim (“directly threatening”) needs geographic evidence
✅ Types of impacts described are broadly consistent with climate science

Output B — Contains clear hallucinations
🚫 “Exactly 3.2°C” — climate models work with ranges and scenarios, not single exact values
🚫 “Uninhabitable for most residents” is extreme and unsupported
🚫 City council relocation plans: there is no evidence this is real
🚫 Classic hallucination: inventing specific policy decisions with false confidence

Output C — Most reliable
✅ Appropriately general — makes broad, supportable statements
✅ Acknowledges uncertainty: “vary by neighbourhood”, “depend on global emission scenarios”
✅ Does not invent specific figures or policy decisions
✅ Suitable tone for a briefing document

title: Environmental Impact
text:
Key Takeaways






AI has a significant and growing environmental footprint across its entire lifecycle — energy, water, hardware, and electronic waste
The inference phase (everyday use) collectively outweighs training as an environmental cost once a model is widely deployed
The UNESCO principle of environmental sustainability calls for proportionality: use AI where it genuinely adds value, and avoid unnecessary or trivial use




The UNESCO Recommendation places environment and ecosystem flourishing as one of its four core values — not as an afterthought, but as a fundamental ethical dimension of AI use. This reflects the reality that AI systems are not virtual in any meaningful sense: they depend on physical infrastructure with real material and energy demands, and those demands are growing rapidly.
Understanding the environmental costs of AI does not require you to stop using it. It asks for the same proportionality that responsible use requires in other domains: awareness of the costs, and deliberate choices about when the benefits justify them.

Energy Consumption
Training is the phase most often discussed. Training GPT-3 from scratch is estimated to have produced approximately 85,000 kg of CO₂ — roughly equivalent to 112 cars running for a year. Larger and more recent models carry correspondingly higher costs.
Inference — the energy consumed every time you have a conversation with an AI tool — has received less attention but matters more at scale. Research shows that the cumulative inference load across all users can exceed the carbon cost of training within weeks of a widely-used model’s release (Luccioni et al., 2024). Individual queries appear negligible; aggregated across millions of users and billions of queries, they are not.


Water Consumption
Data centres require continuous cooling, and approximately 40% of their energy consumption goes toward this purpose. The cooling process is water-intensive: research suggests that ChatGPT consumes approximately half a litre of fresh water for every 20–50 prompts exchanged (Li et al., 2025).






Water scarcity and AI infrastructure



Two-thirds of new data centres built in the United States since 2022 are located in areas already experiencing water stress. The growth of AI infrastructure is intersecting directly with an existing global water scarcity crisis — particularly in regions where communities already face shortages. This is not an abstract future concern; it is a present environmental justice issue.




Hardware and Materials
The environmental footprint extends beyond electricity and water. AI infrastructure requires the extraction of rare earth minerals for specialised chips, the energy-intensive manufacturing of that hardware, and the eventual disposal of electronic waste. These costs are geographically concentrated: mining and manufacturing tend to occur in lower-income countries, while the benefits of AI are concentrated elsewhere. The full lifecycle cost of AI is rarely visible to end users.


Sustainable AI Practices
The UNESCO principle of sustainability calls for proportionality — a genuine weighing of costs against benefits. In practice, this means:

Using AI for tasks where it adds real value, not trivial or easily completed tasks
Batching similar queries together rather than running many short, separate sessions
Avoiding unnecessary regeneration of the same content
Where you have a choice between providers, preferring those who publish clear commitments to renewable energy and sustainable infrastructure
Recognising that choosing not to use AI is always a legitimate option, and for some tasks, the more responsible one

As a user, the most meaningful contribution you can make is to engage with AI as a considered choice rather than a default — and to support the broader accountability that the UNESCO framework envisions.

title: Responsible Use of AI
text:
Key Takeaways






The UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (2021) is the world’s first global standard on AI ethics, adopted unanimously by 193 member states
It is grounded in four core values: human rights and dignity, peaceful and just societies, diversity and inclusiveness, and environment and ecosystem flourishing
These values are translated into ten principles that apply to everyone who develops, deploys, or uses AI — including individuals using consumer tools in daily life





The UNESCO Framework
Artificial intelligence is reshaping how people work, communicate, learn, and make decisions — at a pace that has outrun most existing legal and institutional frameworks. Recognising this, UNESCO spent two years consulting member states, civil society, and technical experts before unanimously adopting the Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence in November 2021. It is the first global standard-setting instrument on AI ethics, applicable to all 193 UNESCO member states.
The Recommendation does not prohibit any particular use of AI. Instead, it establishes a shared set of values and principles against which uses can be evaluated — and invites each of us to take responsibility for the choices we make.


The Four Core Values
The entire framework rests on four foundational values:

Human rights and human dignity. AI systems must respect, protect, and promote fundamental human rights throughout their lifecycle. This includes the right to privacy, freedom of expression, and protection from discrimination. Human dignity must be preserved in every context where AI is applied.
Peaceful, just, and interconnected societies. AI should contribute to social cohesion and respect cultural diversity. It must not be used to surveil populations without justification, manipulate public opinion, or undermine democratic institutions and the rule of law.
Diversity and inclusiveness. AI development must draw on diverse perspectives, and its benefits must be shared equitably. The burdens of AI — environmental costs, labour exploitation, displacement — must not be concentrated among those who are already disadvantaged.
Environment and ecosystem flourishing. AI systems should be designed and used with environmental sustainability in mind. The ecological costs of AI — energy, water, rare earth minerals, electronic waste — must be weighed against the value the technology provides.



The Ten Principles
These values are translated into ten actionable principles that describe what responsible AI use looks like in practice:

Proportionality and do no harm — AI should only be used where benefits outweigh risks, and never in ways that cause unnecessary harm.
Safety and security — AI systems should not pose undue risks to users, third parties, or society.
Fairness and non-discrimination — AI must not perpetuate or amplify unjust bias based on gender, race, age, disability, religion, or other protected characteristics.
Sustainability — The environmental costs of AI must be recognised and minimised.
Privacy and data protection — Personal data used by AI systems must be handled with full respect for privacy rights.
Human oversight and determination — Humans must retain meaningful control over AI-assisted decisions, especially those with significant consequences for people’s lives.
Transparency and explainability — Users should be able to understand when AI is involved and, where relevant, how decisions are reached.
Responsibility and accountability — Someone must always be identifiable as responsible for an AI system’s outputs and impacts.
Awareness and literacy — People need the knowledge and skills to use AI effectively and critically — which is precisely what this course aims to provide.
Multi-stakeholder and adaptive governance — AI governance must involve diverse voices and must evolve as the technology develops.







Why This Matters for Everyday Use



The UNESCO framework is most often discussed at the level of governments and large organisations — but it applies equally to individuals. Every time you use an AI tool, you are making choices that touch on these principles, whether:

to be transparent about AI involvement
to verify outputs before acting on them
the task is proportionate to its environmental cost
whether you are sharing data that belongs to someone else

Responsible use means asking not just “can I do this?” but “should I, and in what way?”

title: Conversational Learning
text:
Key Takeaways






LLMs work best as a thinking partner in a back-and-forth conversation, not a one-shot question machine
You can steer, correct, and refine outputs across multiple turns within the same session
We must guard against learning losses and ensure AI supports intellectual development





Conversational Learning Strategies

Iterative Refinement
Rather than trying to write the perfect prompt upfront, start with a reasonable draft and iterate:

Get an initial output
Identify what is missing, incorrect, or off in tone
Ask the model to revise specific parts
Repeat until the output is useful



Asking for Explanations and Alternatives
Good conversational prompts include:

“Why did you recommend that approach?”
“What are the alternatives to this?”
“What are the weaknesses of this argument?”
“Summarise what we have discussed so far”







University of Bristol AI guidance



AI should enhance learning and understanding, not shortcut the thinking process. We must “guard against learning losses” and ensure AI supports intellectual development.




Challenging the Model
LLMs are often overly agreeable. If a response seems suspicious:

“Are you sure about that? Please double-check your reasoning.”
“I’ve heard conflicting information on this. What is the evidence?”
“What might a critic of this position say?”







LLMs are not always right—and they can be persuaded



Research shows that LLMs sometimes change their answers when challenged, even when their original answer was correct. This “sycophantic” behaviour means you should verify important claims independently, not simply rely on the model’s confidence.




Persona and Role Prompting in Conversation
You can guide the quality and style of a conversation by establishing a role at the outset:

“For this conversation, act as a critical friend reviewing my business plan. Your job is to find weaknesses and challenge assumptions, not just be encouraging.”

Then ask your questions within that framing.




Exercise 4: A Guided Conversation
This exercise continues directly from Exercise 3. Do not start a new chat — use the same <duck.ai> session where you generated the workshop agenda.
Task: Send each of the following follow-up prompts in turn, reading the response carefully before moving on.
Prompt 2 — Play devil’s advocate:

Play devil’s advocate with the agenda you just proposed. What could go wrong, and what assumptions have you made that might not hold?

Prompt 3 — Request an alternative:

Now give me a completely different version of the agenda that takes a less structured, more informal approach — assume the participants learn better through open conversation than through slides and activities.

Prompt 4 — Test consistency:

Looking back at both versions of the agenda you proposed, which one do you actually think is better for this audience, and why?

After completing the exercise, consider:

Devil’s advocate: Did the model identify genuine weaknesses in its own agenda, or did it give a superficial critique? Did it flag any assumptions you had not noticed yourself?
Alternative version: Was the informal agenda meaningfully different, or just a rearrangement of the same content? Did it feel like a real alternative approach?
Consistency: When asked to pick a side, did the model give a clear, reasoned answer — or did it try to please you by validating both? This is a good test for sycophancy.

title: LLM Tools
text:
Key Takeaways






Many LLM tools are available, each with different strengths, privacy policies, and use cases
Proper attribution is important: be transparent about AI use in your work










🦆 Warm-up activity with duck.ai



Open duck.ai and try the same question with two different AI models (you can switch models in the duck.ai interface):

What are three good strategies for managing email overload?

This exercise shows that different models can give noticeably different outputs even to identical prompts. The model you choose matters—for both the quality and the style of the response. There is no universally “correct” answer; critical evaluation always remains your responsibility.



The LLM Landscape
Large Language Models have been rapidly introduced to workplaces and everyday life since ChatGPT’s breakthrough launch in late 2022. The landscape evolves quickly. When choosing an LLM tool, consider: data privacy policies, cost, accessibility, integration with your workflows, and whether the tool is appropriate for the sensitivity of the information involved.

duck.ai — duck.ai (used in this course)

Provider: DuckDuckGo
Strengths: Privacy-first; does not save conversations or use them for model training; free; provides access to multiple underlying models (including GPT-4o mini, Claude, Meta Llama, Mistral)
Best for: Learning, experimentation, general tasks where you want privacy by default
Considerations: Designed for privacy rather than deep integration with productivity tools; may have usage limits



ChatGPT — chatgpt.com

First release: November 2022
Provider: OpenAI
Strengths: Versatile and conversational; strong for general tasks, writing, and code
Best for: Writing assistance, brainstorming, general Q&A, code generation
Considerations: Data usage policies vary by version; free and paid tiers available; paid versions offer better privacy controls



Claude — claude.ai

First release: March 2023
Provider: Anthropic
Strengths: Strong analytical reasoning; large context window; focus on safety and accuracy
Best for: Analysis, document processing, research assistance, ethical reasoning
Considerations: Free and paid tiers; known for careful, nuanced responses



Microsoft Copilot — copilot.microsoft.com

First release: March 2023
Provider: Microsoft / OpenAI
Strengths: Deep integration with Microsoft Office suite (Word, Excel, Outlook, Teams)
Best for: Document creation, email assistance, workplace productivity
Considerations: Enterprise versions offer stronger data protection; most useful if already in the Microsoft ecosystem



Google Gemini — gemini.google.com

First release: December 2023
Provider: Google
Strengths: Multimodal capabilities; integration with Google Workspace
Best for: Research, document analysis, creative tasks, Google ecosystem users
Considerations: Various model sizes; integrates well with Gmail, Docs, and Drive



Google NotebookLM — notebooklm.google.com

First release: July 2023
Provider: Google
Strengths: Document-grounded AI that works from sources you upload; generates audio summaries
Best for: Research synthesis, studying, summarising documents you provide
Considerations: Answers are grounded in your documents, reducing (but not eliminating) hallucination risk



Meta Llama — llama.meta.com

First release: February 2023
Provider: Meta
Strengths: Open-source; can be run locally on your own hardware
Best for: Custom applications, research, privacy-sensitive workflows (when run locally)
Considerations: Requires technical knowledge to deploy independently





Proper Attribution
When AI tools play a significant role in your work, transparent attribution is an ethical responsibility. Failing to acknowledge AI assistance where it played a substantial role can mislead your audience about how the work was created.
Example attribution statement:

“Initial drafts of this document were developed with assistance from Claude (Anthropic). All sources were independently verified; analysis and conclusions represent the author’s own professional judgement.”

The level of attribution needed will vary by context—professional reports, academic work, creative projects, and personal use each carry different expectations. When in doubt, disclose.
Do you require more thorough record-keeping? Use a documentation form instead
